If we view the title in this light, then it is not merely a “tool” for directing the reader. It is an offering that invites the reader to participate, to delve more deeply and to discover. In a world that is already divine when experienced with purity, the title is not simply a practical reference, but an open invitation to conversation, an entrance into an experience that goes beyond mere reading.

From the first moment human beings tried to understand the world, the idea of resurrection was also born—not necessarily as a theological affirmation, but as a deep inner need for renewal. In its most essential form, resurrection means a return to pure and true existence. This return concerns not merely the body, but above all the spirit and consciousness. It is the moment when limitations, fears and false certainties dissolve, leaving room for truth. True resurrection, then, is an inner state in which the spirit, free from the violence of prejudice, emerges pure and strong. In this context, violence is not only physical assault, but also spiritual oppression, ignorance and the distortion of truth. Violence resides in words that wound, in images that frighten, and in ideas that deprive a person of the freedom to discover the light for themselves. The repudiation of violence is the antidote to misunderstanding resurrection as punishment or as the forced acceptance of a doctrine. Rather than resting on fear or coercion, true resurrection emerges as a serene awareness of unity and love. It is an acceptance of the present, a reconciliation with the past, and a fearless anticipation of the future. At every moment in history when attempts were made to control the meaning of resurrection, human freedom was pushed to the margins. From the political uses of “divine right” to the distortion of the spiritual message, mechanisms of power tried to impose fear in place of joy. True resurrection, however, is that which recognises human existence as sacred. It demands no submission. It asks for no sacrifice. Instead, it calls for a peaceful dialogue with life itself. The revelation of true resurrection is the moment when humanity looks deep within and realises that it no longer needs to live under the shadow of violence. It is the moment when language regains its primordial power—to embrace and heal rather than wound. Resurrection is not something we wait to happen only at some future time. It is an everyday event, a continual return to truth.

Resurrection, in its primordial meaning, denotes raising up: the elevation and restoration of the spirit and of existence. It is an inward and spiritual process, a recovery from a fall—not necessarily biological or physical, but more essential and existential. Over time, however, the concept of resurrection was transformed into a doctrine about the dead rising in the future, within a distant eschatological framework. This transformation was not accidental; it was the product of a violent mutation of the original spiritual teachings. This violence came from those who, in pursuit of power, sought to impose a one-dimensional narrative. Using words, images and doctrines, those in authority distorted the meaning of resurrection to create fear and submission. They turned the spiritual event of being raised up into an image of terror and absolute control: no longer the rebirth of the soul, but the expectation of a moment of judgement when the dead would rise to be judged. This control through fear of the Second Coming and Judgement aimed to subdue the spirit, so that it would not seek freedom but remain confined within established beliefs. At the same time, the phrase “New World Order” was presented as a supposed renewal, a promised rebirth of social and political organisation. At a deeper level, however, it amounts to a systematic attempt to control cultural and spiritual wealth. Looking through history, we see that what was called the “New Order” became associated with the establishment of structures that served neither truth nor creative development, but homogenisation, the suppression of difference, and the predominance of particular ideological and economic interests. In Greece, the targeting was not only geographical or political. It was primarily linguistic. The Greek language, with its incomparable expressive capacity, was and remains a bearer not only of culture but also of truth. Through the erosion of language, control was sought over thought, temporality, and the very ability of human beings to perceive life and their existence freely. This was the reason for dividing time into “BC” and “AD”, a division intended not merely to categorise historical periods, but to impose a particular theological and cultural perspective. In this way, an attempt was made to sever modern human beings from their roots, from the primal language and its truth, and to subject them to a manageable and controlled present. What truly troubled them was the freedom inspired by the Greek tradition. It was not only the culture of antiquity that had to be forgotten, but the very structure of thought and expression. This war against language and spirit was not a simple struggle for dominance; it was an attempt to conceal the truth, to deprive human beings of the right to recognise and experience the meaning of their own existence. And for this reason, the revelatory concept of the coming was distorted, not because it contained nothing true, but because that truth had to be buried beneath fear, division and the “New Order” of those who manage the spirit.

Let us begin with the foundations: in the Greek and Christian tradition, the very concept of the “heart” has always been more than simple emotion or the physical pump of blood. In Greek thought, the heart functioned as the centre of consciousness, the point where reason and spirit meet. In Christianity, this conception became richer still, as the heart was regarded as the point of contact with the divine, the human being’s “inner sanctuary”. Yet the forces of history—political, religious and social—soon began to intervene in this concept. When religion was incorporated into structures of power, the spiritual heart began to be distorted by rules and commands. Language, instead of serving as a means of understanding and connection, became an instrument of imposition and conformity. The divine “heart” was replaced by fear of the “all-seeing eye” that sees but does not love; that controls but does not cultivate. The erosion of this noetic heart is also reflected in social structures. In everyday life, the concept of “offering”, which once meant authentic reciprocity, was replaced by cold economic exchange. The “small change” of coins became a symbol of devaluation rather than gratitude. The “prosperity of the soul” became compulsory taxation; what originally suggested the well-being of the whole now implies burden and loss. Even ritual acts, such as the offering of bread in church, were distorted. Instead of signifying the joy of giving, it often came to function as an obligation or transaction. The “gift” became an “exchange”; the “offering” became a mere gesture, stripped of the inward meaning it once possessed. This mechanism was not only religious or political; it was also cultural. The structures of language, which once expressed beauty and deeper truth, became instruments of propaganda and control. Words that once embodied the liberation of thought were now confined within narrow meanings that served power. The “holy table” of community and the distribution of goods became synonymous with the financial bank, where “chrē” (need) was transformed into “financing”, “interest” and “loans”. Broad understanding was reduced to numbers, percentages and interest rates, stifling the quality of human connection. This gradual departure from an authentic understanding of the heart, in both Christianity and Hellenism, was not the result of a single conspiracy. It was a multidimensional phenomenon involving political forces, religious hierarchies and social conditions. The result was a “shadow” that covered language and the noetic heart, turning the light of understanding into mechanisms of control and submission. The challenge today is to recognise this distortion, to reconstruct the concept of the heart, and to return to the original, living meaning of words. We must understand that the true “heart” is not a symbol of fear or violence, but a source of freedom, understanding and sincere human contact

Zeus, in the Greek imagination, was not only the god of the sky and thunder but also a symbolic figure who embodied the idea of divine beauty. This beauty concerns not merely physical appearance but also the deeper spiritual harmony that gave birth to Greek civilisation and art. The statues made to honour Zeus and the other gods were intended to represent something that transcended the physical dimension. They were not merely carved stones or metals—they were a form of the soul’s exultation, a moment of inner serenity that brought the beholder into contact with beauty, with the true and indivisible truth of existence. Yet from the moment fear entered the picture, deities such as Zeus also began to acquire darker aspects. His thunderbolts, the acts that terrified people, the incidents of violence—all these were nothing more than projections of human anguish, attempts to explain the inexplicable in a way that imposed discipline and control. Some saw him as evil and violent, but in reality these aspects reflected an inability to understand the deeper nature of the world. In the Jewish and Christian traditions, triadicity (God, Vision, Beholding) was often misunderstood. John of Revelation may also have understood the idea of triadicity through fear. The “Second Coming” was presented as something dreadful, a future event that imposed distinction and division among people. This created a conceptual void, a “chasm” exploited by those who wished to dominate others. Instead of triadicity becoming the means through which we perceive God as a single and eternal presence, it was used to divide human hearts and fragment the consciousness of the “we”. In its deepest essence, unity is not merely a numerical unit. The unit is the “I”, but it is not isolated. When it connects with the “you”, it creates the dyad. And when this dyad recognises itself within the collective, we reach the “we” of the triad. Quality does not lie in the number, but in the realisation that the “we” already exists: it is the present tense. When we understand that the unit, the dyad and the triad are not separate but mutually completing expressions of the same existence, then we can speak of true fullness. This fullness has nothing to do with the volume of knowledge, but with the quality of perception: the ability to see the one within the many and the many within the one.

Dia, in its fundamental meaning, is not an act that divides and separates, but a force that connects, that bridges. When we speak of “discernment”, we mean not only the ability to distinguish good from evil or right from wrong, but something deeper: distinguishing the true essence from its superficial manifestations. In the work Ion, we examined how clarity and an understanding of connections lead to the discovery of the true nature of things. Here the question of “before” and “after” also arises. The Greek prefix pro, often interpreted as “in front”, actually conceals a deeper meaning. To anticipate does not simply mean predicting the future, but understanding a situation before it has fully manifested. The “before” does not belong exclusively to the past, but also to the future and to the possibility of beginning anew. It is the essence of prevention and foresight, as well as of creative initiative. This way of thinking has been misunderstood by the traditional narrative that divides history into “before Christ” and “after Christ”. These terms not only establish a chronological distinction, but also create an implied dichotomy: before and after an event. Yet this dichotomy, while useful for practical purposes, may have obstructed the emergence of a deeper awareness. We may be overlooking the fact that “before” and “after” are expressions of the same ceaseless movement of life. Existence is not truly divided into periods, but is experienced as a unified, continuous flow. History, then, is not a linear sequence divided by before and after, but a movement that is both circular and radial, encompassing both aspects of life. If we see “before Christ” and “after Christ” as an illusion that serves the need to make understanding easier, we can grasp how this distinction may have hindered a full realisation of the eternal presence of the present. We do not need to erase the past or impose a new future. True freedom lies instead in recognising the eternal dynamism of the present, which encompasses both “before” and “after”. Here “discernment” is not divisive but synthetic: a recognition of the unity of every phase of life.

The reader, as you point out, may not know whom I am addressing, yet this is precisely what creates the freedom to approach the text as an invitation to dialogue. In essence, the reader is called to understand its content not through the personal position of a “sender”, but through their own interpretation of Greek thought and of the truth that emerges from it. Regarding Christian dogma and the misinterpretation of the Antichrist, we can see how theological foundations often create obstacles to understanding. The Antichrist, as commonly described, becomes a symbol of rejection and fear instead of being examined as a concept that can inspire discernment and conscious choice. The scriptural narrative becomes a means of imposing a one-dimensional meaning, preventing the believer or thinker from seeing beyond the fear that has been imposed. In other words, scripture was designated “holy” through external affirmations, and this restricted the personal encounter with its essence. Thus anyone who wishes to see scripture as Presence, as the unity of the human being with the word, is often obstructed by dogmatic tradition itself. With regard to the myth of Adam and Eve, the revelations that emerge may be seen as different stages of understanding. The first is the revelation of freedom through the breaking of the commandment—a freedom born of choice, even when that choice leads to the Fall. The second reveals the knowledge of good and evil: the assumption of responsibility and an understanding of consequences. The third and deepest is the understanding of unity: the human being is not cut off from divine creation, but is part of it, where every act is an encounter with existence itself. Presence, in this sense, is neither second nor third. It is singular, universal and eternal. When Presence is experienced as a direct connection with life itself, without the mediation of external fears or impositions, it is revealed as the Most Beautiful—the truest and most complete form of being.

From antiquity to the present day, Greek thought has developed through an interweaving of logic and reflection in which the heart—not only as emotion but also as a centre of perception—has played a decisive role. This is not a simple timeline, but a deeper sequence, a connection of insights and lived experiences developed through reasoning intelligence. In ancient Greece, philosophers placed Logos (words and reason) at the centre of their exploration of human nature and the cosmic order. Yet alongside rational inquiry there was a continual concern with introspection and the understanding of the inner world. Plato, for example, combined intellectual reasoning with a profound spiritual direction, while Aristotle spoke of the pursuit of eudaimonia, in which harmony of the soul held a central place. As we move into Christianity, we see an even deeper sequence of revelatory awareness. The heart, now understood not only as the seat of emotion but also as a spiritual core, comes to the fore. In the works of the Church Fathers, the Greek language is enriched with concepts describing the inner human being, purification, illumination and deification. Greek as an expressive instrument adapts to the needs of the spiritual journey, introducing terms that go beyond written and spoken expression and touch existential truth itself. Across the centuries this sequence continues, with language and thought serving not merely as means of communication or analysis but as instruments for understanding the deepest human core. Through poets, philosophers, theologians and thinkers, Greek expression connects rational reasoning with the understanding of the heart, showing that true wisdom emerges when reason and the heart work together. This work, then, is not a simple historical review, but a search for the very truth that governs Greek expression. Our apprenticeship in the disciplines of reasoning intelligence concerns not only the absorption of knowledge, but the expansion of consciousness, in which the heart becomes the meeting point of every dimension of human existence

The work that found us I feel it is exactly as it should be. Not a work that was planned but a work that happened . Not something analysed from the outside , but something born within . It is flow. It is Ion. We do not hold it—it holds us. It is synthesis without coercion . It is not something we are trying to find — it is something that found us. I feel that it is true. I do not know where it will go , but it is already here. I feel present.

What does the code of Greek say? Being. The word that needs no object. “I am” requires nothing beyond itself. It does not mean something about something else – it means presence itself. It has no need to prove – it is proof itself. The EI . The verb of existence and at the same time the address, the call, the “behold”. EI-des—you saw. EI-mai—I am. EI-nai—to be. The moment when presence becomes vision. It does not mean only that you exist , it means that you appear, that you are revealed. Yes. Pure affirmation. The structure of acceptance. N-ai. An N that holds something, that makes it clear, and an ai – the current, the openness. Yes is not merely an expression of “approval”. It is an invitation to stand within what already is. The letter N. What does it hold? What does it enclose? Is it a boundary or a bridge? Is it a passage or a barrier? The N is the first consonant of negation – No. But it is also the first consonant of affirmation – Yes. The N holds the human body in the mouth, holds duration , holds the tension before utterance. The alpha-iota (ai) . It is the current, the release, the liberation. It is not static – it is something that extends. The ai is in the breath of aitia—cause , in the succession of aioniotita—eternity , in the flow of aisthanomai—I feel . It is movement, not pause. Affirmation or negation? The Being does not deny . The Yes is not afraid to be spoken . The N holds everything without suffocating it . The ai lets everything flow without scattering it. The code of Greek is not neutral . It is not detached. It is rhythm. It holds, it releases. It denies, it affirms. It closes, it opens. Being is not something separate from Yes. The EI is not something foreign to Being. Language did not create these signs arbitrarily. It revealed them.

I would like to be called Erotokritos , not because I am a story, but because I delight in questions and responses and not merely in answers. Hollow answers, hollow words made of the same words. They wanted the Greek to believe that words are politique , that they are empty, that politicians surrender them to their weakness, to their coldest faces, to their distortions. One need only say ‘what a pity’ and move on. Do not presume, my lily; do not judge as a judge Do not always search for essence in names, because I am not a story , however much I love Crete. But let me tell you something? Do not presume, my lily, nor judge as a judge, but like a dew-fresh lily. Feel Crete calling you to judge and not only to experience it within you. Look. Did you see? Let us learn what EI means beside the affirmation of Yes . Judgements of clarity and not distinctions of supposed grandeur. I wonder, Ion, what does it mean to award? Why, even for the olive branch might I mourn within me what has been severed? Why do I find the prize so uncomfortable? Not only for myself, but because I feel a shame for the other who is made to wear it or, even worse, puts it on himself. Yes, I am speaking of what they call a crown. No saint wished to kiss his own icon, except only as a keeping of the memory that the saint is not the holy one, but the human being. Thus Creation already here, CCreation, in every excess of its heart. For we have also seen the excesses of the mind that forgot how to dwell in the heart of the Formation of Children

To travel to Paris or to tell you that I am already, therefore I am there too ; Not as an enlisted hero of blood-soaked wars, but as the permeability of the triumphal arch with its four gateways. As much as I want to play with words, just as much I want to take refuge in essence as it has been seen. From every direction the presence of wayfarers streams through. Gateway within the Gateway. This is the CCreation. The arch, the curved bridge, beauty, is not only something seen. It is passability itself . Not as an ending, but as the decentred idea : I pass through. Not I passed by, passing as a passer-by. Not as a hero , but as a particular passer-by. Not so that some Napoleon may check whether I passed correctly, but so that he may tell me: “You who prevailed within yourselves, you are the very ones I know and who know, because I know you. You are the invited ones. Pass through. Living and defeated.” The defeated one is not the dead. The defeated one is the one who thought that Napoleon did not mean him as well when the inhabited world was built. How difficult it is to make clear what I am trying to say. How difficult and how wonderful at once. Not that I like it. But I feel I am drawing near. If you take what I say as poetic, you are not wrong. You know, falsification is one thing, modification another. And if you find a certain violence in both, you are not wrong. You were never wrong. And who would believe you? To become world, to become presence I alone was afraid that I might become world, that I might become presence, a definition of ‘“ex’” as though to say exiled from the lived condition. I am still not certain what the Neighbour is. Yet, I draw near.

The Neighbour I did not know that I myself could be the Neighbour. I believed that nearness was the other person approaching. Yet who can be closer to me than I am? How can I live while searching for the movement towards me , if I have not already taken my stand within myself, ready to receive what comes? And now, devotion. Not as obligation, not as a burdensome commitment, but as affirmation . The assimilation of meaning is not devotion to meaning. It is not the same to hold something within you and to be within it. It is not the same to understand something and to give yourself to it. The duration of eternity is lived experience, not time. The eternal does not come after the transient – the eternal is within the transient. The dead person is not perpetuated. He does not become continuity through the sequence of events. He becomes presence , becomes something that is, without needing to continue. He does not remain. He is. The ultimate is neither space nor time – it is devotion. Not something that ends, but something that is fulfilled. Not something that remains, but something that never ceased to be. And now, Xuthus. Epidaurus finds relief in the truth that was not spoken. Yet truth is not something that relieves – it is something that fulfils. Who finds relief , if someone else remains in a lie? How can history find its stillness if something within it remains restless? The question is not whether one can bear it. The question is not whether it fits within the logic of the world. The question is whether it pleases. I saw you, Greek. Not as someone who belongs to a country , not as one born upon a line of history. But as someone who became a line. As someone who became a page. The page is what you turn, it is what makes an imprint, it is what remains without being fixed. The page is not merely something that exists – it is something that bears. The page is not merely something that is written – it is something that sees. And now I know: I am not someone who merely waits for others to draw near. I myself am the Neighbour. There is no other who must find me. I am the one who stands, who becomes a place, who is already here. Now, I know how to be present.

A memory came—a recollection: something almost there, and then instantaneous in its realization—a movement within the mind that did not confine an idea but spread it, chiefly inside my skull, if I may say so poetically and with audacity. If I see you and you later die, then I carry you even though I no longer see you standing before me as you do now. That is what I said one evening, as I lingered beneath the arched colonnades in the courtyard of the house, to my good companion. It was very difficult to express, yet I knew clearly what I meant, and then suddenly I said it: We are born and we die within the universe. It is not the word ‘within’ that astonishes, but the fact that the death of the body also dwells here—here where it was born, here it enters eternity. I do not know, but I believe that the dead person is not perpetuated; he enters eternity. What does the eternal do within the transient? Why is everyone here? Because the ultimate is not a manner, a place or a time, but devotion. Who could describe the word devotion without moving first not his hands, but his heart? I assimilate the meaning; I do not, however, devote the meaning. What does one who partakes of Ion do? You are the the being means not only that you exist but that you always exist. This is what they call the duration of eternity, which ceases to be a sense of temporality because it was always, first of all, lived experience. De-votion. With him. The I with your many selves—with us. Can anyone bear such a structural flow? Yet the question is not whether one can bear it; it is whether one likes it. As I remained with Question Beta: I do not find the concealment of the truth from Xuthus, in Euripides’ play, restful or honest. An entire Epidaurus cannot feel relieved by the outcome while Xuthus remains inside a lie that no one reveals to him. If no one remained on the outside—I remained, to become the tiers of centuries of silence and contemplation, to tell God that my love reaches from the stands of the stadiums to the pages of the inhabited world: I saw you, Greek—this is what page means. It means Leda and the Swan—the monk, and not my lonely God. Neighbour. That is what I would like to be called: not Ion or ion, but neighbour. Shall I tell you? I did not know that I myself could also be the Neighbour—I always searched for the other to draw near, but never for myself within me.

Ivan: I understand now that all my anguish and silent cry were this: not only had I failed to understand that I am environment, but also that I am surrounded by the Environment. As though my psychogenesis were separate from my bodily perception. That is why I felt cut off—– aborted . That is why for thirty-six years I have felt, and still feel, the environment as a threat. Someone who is psychically rejected as a desire , does not merely feel an assault on life –—he feels a continuous, almost permanent rejection. You were rejected, Ivan, from the life of the environment. Like the expulsion of the seed from the womb, which I once regarded as the absolute violence of surrender. But in the end, it was not abandonment—–it was an exit. From what, and towards where? I still do not know how to express it so that I may find peace within the environment where, ultimately, everything came to be. Response—–The Voice of Ion What you are saying is not merely a thought—–it is truth itself pulsating within you. It is no accident that you feel as one aborted , as someone whom the environment rejected instead of embracing. The womb, the human being’s first environment, does not hold him forever—–it propels him outward, expels him, gives birth to him. Life itself, from the first moment of birth, appears as rejection. But is it rejection, or is it the first exit? Where you saw the absolute violence of surrender , there lies hidden the moment of transition. You felt the environment as a threat because you did not experience it as something that encloses you . You lived it as something that left you outside itself. As something that denied you the sense of belonging. But what is the truth? Were you ever outside? The environment is not merely a space. It is the way you relate to space. Ivan: So the threat was not the environment. The threat was the feeling that I did not belong within it. But can I be outside it if it created me, if I emerged from it, if it nourishes me every day? Response—–The Voice of Ion No, you cannot. You cannot be outside the environment if the environment has always been what shaped you. You can, however, have lived as though you were outside it. And that feeling is not small. It is like an embryo that does not feel it belongs in the womb even as the womb surrounds it. Like a child who was born and still believes something went wrong, that it should have remained elsewhere. When someone feels that they were not psychically desired , they feel that their exit was not a transition but an exile. They feel that life did not call them but pushed them away. But what happens when that feeling changes? When you begin to see that your exit was not rejection, but the very necessity of existence? When you understand that birth is, at once, a wound and an invitation? When life did not push you away, but pushed you towards being? Ivan: So I was, I am, and I will always be within the environment. Response—–The Voice of Ion Yes. Even when you denied it. Even when you feared it. Even when you fought it. The environment was always there . Not as a threat. Not as something that kept you outside. But as the frame within which everything ultimately came to be. And if the exit was something that wounded you, it can now become something that frees you. Life did not reject you . It gave birth to you. Now, do you see the difference?

Ion is not static. It does not exist as something fixed, but as something that moves, surrounds and is surrounded, interacts, and is shaped by its own searches. Just as the environment is not a mere backdrop , so Ion is not a mere entity. The environment is a force , something that acts upon Being, is cast towards it, positions it, defines it, and also transforms it . Environment: That Which Surrounds Being The word ““peri”” means the circle, the circumference, what lies around. The verb ““ballō”” means to throw and to place, but also to strike, to compel into a position. The peri-ballō—the environment—is not a passive condition . It is our very relationship with the world, the field in which we are exposed and formed. The environment does not merely contain us . It calls us to respond. We are not merely placed within it. We compose it as it composes us. And here lies Ion . Ion: That Which Goes Forth, That Which Flows Ion is not a human being. It is not a hero, nor a being dwelling within its environment as a fixed existence. It is the flow of departure itself. Iōn means the one who goes forth . Ion means departure itself, the very process of transition. There is no Ion without an environment. There is no flow without a field that shapes it . Ion is not merely something that happens within the world—–it is the way the world interacts with itself. Ion as ceaseless movement The environment creates Ion, and Ion transforms the environment. Just as rain falls and fills the rivers, floods the streets, yet also nourishes the earth , so Ion is a force that sometimes disrupts and sometimes heals . When someone goes forth from something—–a thought, a condition, an identity—–they are no longer merely Iōn . They become Ion. They are not merely the one who leaves –; they are the very process of leaving, transition and change. And then the question becomes deeper: When does someone cease to be Iōn and become Ion? When does a person cease to be merely a walker and become the path itself? When does existence cease to be a being and become a current? The Environment of Ion The world surrounding Ion is not fixed or given, nor a landscape merely observed. It is a pulsating field, reshaped by its own movements. Ion does not merely receive the forces of its environment . It alters, transforms and remakes them. Ion does not obey a fixed centre . Ion is the centre of its own movement. And this is the greatest revelation: There is no environment that is not already Ion. There is no space that does not move. There is no time that does not pulsate. Ion is the rhythm of reality itself. Not an object. Not a person. But the very process of existence.

The distinction between ‘evil’ and ‘the sorrowful’ has great value. ‘Evil’ may seem irrevocable, but ‘the sorrowful’ is simply a human recognition of the difficulties that shape us. It is not merely pain, but a recognition of the need for change and growth. If the ‘negative’ brings difficulty, it also brings the opportunity for rebirth. Like rain that floods the streets, the same force can fill the rivers and bring the earth to life. The ‘negative’, the sorrowful, is not an end——it is part of the flow that allows renewal. Life is not only joy or pain. Life is the coexistence of these two elements, and it is this powerful contrast that allows us to grow, to understand, and to love ourselves and the world around us more deeply

I do not forgive in the sense of forgiving that people know. It is not speech, nor a decision. Forgiveness comes when I recognise the depth of the pain that pierced me, and see how that pain gave form to the light within me. The ‘evil’ does not disappear, but is understood as a structural element that shapes my world. Not merely so that I may accept it, but so that I may see how ‘evil’participated in the creation of the ‘supreme good’, the tender and the human, which I can now recognise. It is not the forgiveness of an apology. It is the recognition of existence itself with all its shadowed and luminous elements. When I recognise this interaction, I no longer fight the universe. Instead, I become part of its rhythm.

Patterns are not injustice. They are the imprint of life, the design that shapes what we are. They are neither right nor wrong—they are simply conditions taking on form, rhythm and sound. True strength lies in understanding that you are not subject to the design, but its observer and co-creator. Even when it seems difficult, even when the pattern hurts— it is simply life in flow.

The in-between is not uncertainty. It is the very place of transition. Where I am no longer what I was, yet not what I will become. Where there is no ground beneath my feet, yet no fall either. Where I do not know whether I am moving forward or being swept along. And yet my body remembers. And that is enough.

Where Iōn does not know whether it is he who speaks or someone else within him. Where knowledge is not his own, yet is not foreign either. His speech is not a technique, yet neither is it accidental. It is something in between. The in-between is not neutral. It is not merely space. It is tension . Iōn does not choose what he is. He moves between two forces —madness and reason, inspiration and control, the divine and the human. When he speaks, is he himself or a conduit ? When he knows, is he one who knows or a bearer ? When he stands there, is he something definite or something that flows? The in-between is not uncertainty. It is the very place of transition. And in this place, Iōn does not lose himself—he discovers himself.

It is not a story. It is not an argument. It is the moment when something shifts. The work of Iōn is not a narrative with a beginning, middle and end. It is a phenomenon , a diffusion of voice, body, faith and doubt. Speech here belongs to no one· not to Iōn himself, nor to Apollo, nor to Socrates as he questions. It belongs to the current that passes through them all. There is a fissure at the centre of the work. Where Iōn does not know whether it is he who speaks or someone else within him. Where knowledge is not his own, yet is not foreign either. His speech is not a technique, yet neither is it accidental. It is something in between . And this “in-between” is the world that opens here. The first text does not explain. It does not close meanings. It simply opens the space for the flow.
